title: TheGreenFeed Deterministic Survey Analysis Framework (v4)
purpose: A versioned rules-and-interpretation file for turning aggregate v4 survey responses into transparent findings and practical next steps. Dimensions stay separate; categorical answers are never summed into a score.

dominance.closeSplit: top two options differ by < 10 percentage points; describe as mixed
dominance.tie: two or more options share the highest count
dominance.smallSampleWarning: For N < 10, show descriptive counts but label interpretation preliminary.

guardrails: Use cautious language: may indicate, is consistent with, suggests.
Never claim causation from this cross-sectional self-report survey.
Do not infer why a student chose an answer unless the survey asked why.
Do not treat missing answers as an option value.
Show N and counts alongside percentages; small percentage differences are not automatically meaningful.
Compare related questions before recommending an intervention.
Do not claim respondents represent all PCTE students unless the sampling method supports that.
Separate observed facts from interpretation and recommendations.
Confidence is not knowledge; knowledge is not behaviour; a stated intention is not an action.

rules: Because name and course are collected, do not call responses anonymous.
Keep names and phone numbers out of aggregate analysis and analysis exports.
Raw response export contains identifying data and must be admin-only.
Suppress or combine very small programme groups in breakdowns.

questions.construct: Reported frequency of encountering improper disposal

a.label: Never
a.interpretation: Low reported exposure to improper disposal in the respondent's usual areas.

b.label: Rarely
b.interpretation: Low reported exposure; may reflect cleaner routes or lower exposure.

c.label: Sometimes
c.interpretation: An intermittent or location-specific problem may be present.

d.label: Often
d.interpretation: A visible problem may warrant hotspot checks and direct observation.

e.label: Very often
e.interpretation: A frequently reported problem; pair with q2 to locate perceived hotspots.

questions.analysisCaveat: Self-reported perception, not an objective waste audit or proof of actual conditions.

a.label: Canteens, food areas or student gathering spots
a.interpretation: Inspect food packaging, peak traffic, bin access and collection frequency.

b.label: Classrooms, corridors or other shared indoor areas
b.interpretation: Review indoor bin access, labels, routines and cleaning schedules.

c.label: Outdoor areas, pathways or other places around campus
c.interpretation: Review outdoor bin placement, high-traffic paths and wind-blown litter.

d.label: Not sure
d.interpretation: The respondent cannot name a hotspot; do not treat this as 'no problem'.

questions.analysisCaveat: Identifies broad perceived areas, not exact locations; a genuine 'not sure' is not a location.

a.label: Never
a.interpretation: Strong reported access barrier; verify against a physical bin audit.

c.label: Sometimes
c.interpretation: Intermittent access; may be location- or time-dependent.

d.label: Often
d.interpretation: Access is generally reported as adequate.

e.label: Always
e.interpretation: Access is consistently reported as adequate.

f.label: Not sure
f.interpretation: The respondent cannot judge availability; not evidence of a barrier either way.

questions.analysisCaveat: Perceived access only; the survey cannot measure whether a bin physically exists, its capacity or collection schedule.

c.label: Sometimes
c.interpretation: Intermittent overflow; could be peak-load or collection timing.

d.label: Often
d.interpretation: Frequent reported overflow; may indicate capacity or collection gaps.

e.label: Always
e.interpretation: Consistent reported overflow; a strong capacity/collection signal to verify.

f.label: Not sure
f.interpretation: The respondent cannot judge; not evidence of overflow either way.

questions.analysisCaveat: Reported perception, not measured waste volumes or an audit of bin capacity and collection.

a.label: Clear everywhere
a.interpretation: Labels are reported as clear across campus.

b.label: Clear in some places only
b.interpretation: Inconsistent labelling; check the areas that are less clear.

c.label: Not clear
c.interpretation: Labels are reported as unclear; a labelling gap is plausible.

d.label: No labels
d.interpretation: Labels are reported as absent in the places the respondent uses.

e.label: Not sure
e.interpretation: The respondent has not registered the labels; not evidence of clarity.

questions.analysisCaveat: Perceived label clarity; does not test whether the labels match the real campus waste streams.

a.label: It is not a problem
a.interpretation: Respondent does not see littering as a problem; a normative or awareness issue may exist.

b.label: I dislike it but it is common
b.interpretation: Disapproval alongside a perceived norm of littering.

c.label: I dislike it and think it should be addressed
c.interpretation: Strong personal disapproval; an attitude, not observed behaviour.

questions.analysisCaveat: A stated attitude, not a behaviour; social-desirability bias is likely.

questions.construct: Reported usual disposal behaviour when a bin is inconvenient

a.label: Leave it near the nearest bin
a.interpretation: A reported littering behaviour when a bin is inconvenient.

b.label: Look for another bin
b.interpretation: A reported effort to find an appropriate bin.

c.label: Keep it with me until I find a bin
c.interpretation: A reported effort to hold waste until a bin is found.

d.label: Take it away with me
d.interpretation: A reported effort to carry waste and dispose of it later.

questions.analysisCaveat: Self-reported behaviour, not observed conduct; option wording aims to avoid making one answer sound virtuous.

a.label: Almost none
a.interpretation: The respondent believes very few peers dispose properly.

b.label: A minority
b.interpretation: The respondent believes a minority of peers dispose properly.

d.label: A majority
d.interpretation: The respondent believes most peers dispose properly.

e.label: Almost all
e.interpretation: The respondent believes nearly all peers dispose properly.

f.label: Not sure
f.interpretation: No formed perception; not evidence of a norm either way.

questions.analysisCaveat: Perceived norm, not measured behaviour of classmates.
A stated intention, not observed behaviour; the survey does not ask why some would stay silent.

questions.section: Do campus rules and messages reach students?

a.label: Yes, I knew about both
a.interpretation: Reported awareness, not proof of understanding or effectiveness.

b.label: I knew about one of these, but not the other
b.interpretation: Partial awareness may point to incomplete or unclear communication.

c.label: No, I did not know about either
c.interpretation: Rules may not be reaching many respondents.

questions.analysisCaveat: Reported awareness only; does not show enforcement works or that fines change behaviour. Verify the real rule wording with the institution.

questions.section: Do campus rules and messages reach students?
questions.construct: Communication funnel: exposure, recall and actionability

a.label: I have not noticed any
a.interpretation: No reported exposure; placement, salience or reach may be limiting.

b.label: I noticed some, but cannot recall what they asked me to do
b.interpretation: Exposure without recall; messages may not be memorable or actionable.

c.label: I recall a message and roughly what it asked

d.label: I recall a message and knew what to do and where
d.interpretation: Recall and reported actionability; recall does not prove behaviour change.

questions.analysisCaveat: Each stage is respondent-reported; this does not audit how often or where the college actually communicates.

questions.section: Do campus rules and messages reach students?

a.label: Little or none
a.interpretation: May indicate an education or communication gap.

b.label: Some guidance, but not enough to feel consistent or practical
b.interpretation: Guidance may be too abstract, occasional or disconnected from disposal points.

c.label: Enough practical guidance to understand what I should do
c.interpretation: Perceived adequacy; check against q13 and the real campus streams.

questions.analysisCaveat: Reported guidance, not a test of actual knowledge.

questions.section: Do campus rules and messages reach students?

a.label: Not confident; I am unsure how to separate them correctly
a.interpretation: Practical, item-specific guidance may help; confidence is not accuracy.

b.label: Somewhat confident, but unsure about at least one item
b.interpretation: Targeted guidance on confusing items may be useful.

c.label: Confident that I know how to separate all three
c.interpretation: High self-reported confidence; actual sorting accuracy remains untested.

questions.analysisCaveat: Confidence, not knowledge; the survey contains no verified answer key for the campus streams.

questions.section: What could help, and what to test next

a.label: Bins are missing, full or unclear
a.interpretation: Infrastructure is named as the main obstacle; verify with an audit.

b.label: Students lack awareness or guidance
b.interpretation: Knowledge/guidance is named as the main obstacle.

c.label: Poor habits / social norms
c.interpretation: Norms/habits are named as the main obstacle.

d.label: No single obstacle stands out
d.interpretation: The respondent does not single out one barrier; not proof there is no problem.

e.label: Not sure
e.interpretation: No formed view; not evidence of no problem.

questions.analysisCaveat: A single perceived barrier; the wording no longer bundles infrastructure problems or reads as a non-answer.

questions.section: What could help, and what to test next

a.label: Better bins, placement and labels
a.interpretation: Infrastructure and clear sorting cues are preferred.

b.label: Clear, practical sorting guidance
b.interpretation: Practical education is preferred over broad awareness messaging.

c.label: Visible peer-led habits and activities
c.interpretation: A voluntary peer-led pilot may be worth testing.

d.label: Stricter enforcement of the rules
d.interpretation: Enforcement is preferred; verify the real rules and how they are applied before acting.

questions.analysisCaveat: A preference and a hypothesis, not evidence of what is effective or affordable.

questions.section: What could help, and what to test next

a.label: Short videos / social posts
a.interpretation: A digital short-form pilot may be worth testing.

b.label: Posters and signs near bins
b.interpretation: Point-of-decision prompts may be worth testing.

c.label: Live demonstrations or events
c.interpretation: Interactive formats may appeal; evaluate access, cost and participation.

d.label: Class announcements
d.interpretation: An institutional channel may be worth testing.

questions.analysisCaveat: Preferred channel is a hypothesis, not a measured effective channel.

questions.section: What could help, and what to test next

b.label: Here is exactly what goes where
b.interpretation: Specific practical instructions may be more useful than broad appeals.

c.label: Here are the rules and penalties
c.interpretation: Rule-based messaging may resonate; verify policy wording and pair it with accessible bins.

d.label: Your classmates are doing it
d.interpretation: A social-norm frame may resonate; avoid shaming or exaggeration.

questions.analysisCaveat: A preference, not proof the message would change behaviour.

questions.section: What could help, and what to test next

a.label: Nothing at the moment
a.interpretation: No participation intended; reasons were not asked.

b.label: Share or repost a message
b.interpretation: A low-effort online form of participation.

c.label: Join a short one-off campus activity
c.interpretation: Interest in a bounded, low-commitment activity.

d.label: Help run an activity or team
d.interpretation: Interest in a larger voluntary role; confirm with sign-ups.

questions.analysisCaveat: Stated willingness, not actual sign-up or attendance.

sectionAnalysis.label: Campus conditions and convenience
sectionAnalysis.purpose: Describe reported visibility of improper disposal, perceived hotspots, and reported bin access, overflow and label clarity.

patterns.when: q1 option d or e is common
patterns.meaning: Respondents frequently report encountering improper disposal; pair with q2 to identify perceived hotspots.
actions: Check hotspots directly at busy and quiet times
Audit bins in the leading perceived area

patterns.when: q3 option a or b is common
patterns.meaning: Many respondents report that a bin is rarely or never available and easy to reach.
actions: Audit bin placement and access in the perceived hotspots
Distinguish missing bins from hard-to-reach ones before spending

patterns.when: q4 option d or e is common
patterns.meaning: Many respondents report that bins are often or always full or not emptied often enough.
actions: Review collection frequency and capacity at peak times
Check overflow at the leading perceived hotspot

patterns.when: q5 option c or d is common
patterns.meaning: Respondents report that bin labels are unclear or absent where they use bins.
actions: Audit label presence and legibility
Confirm labels match the real campus waste streams before relabelling

patterns.when: q7 option a is common and (q3 option a/b or q4 option d/e is common)
patterns.meaning: Reported littering near bins coincides with reported access or capacity problems.
actions: Audit bin access, capacity, placement and labels
Pilot a targeted improvement at one hotspot

cautions: Survey reports are not a campus waste audit.
q2 identifies broad perceived areas, not exact locations.
'Not sure' answers in q3/q4/q5 are not evidence of a problem or of its absence.

sectionAnalysis.label: Attitudes, norms and reported behaviour
sectionAnalysis.purpose: Describe personal attitude to littering, reported usual behaviour, perceived peer norms and stated willingness to intervene — kept as separate constructs.

patterns.when: q6 option c is common and q8 option a or b is common
patterns.meaning: Respondents disapprove of littering but believe few classmates dispose properly — an attitude/norm gap.
actions: Test visible peer-modelling rather than blaming language
Measure whether a norm message changes perceived norms over time

patterns.when: q9 options a+b exceed q9 options d+e
patterns.meaning: More respondents are unlikely to intervene than likely; the survey does not ask why.
actions: Offer respectful, non-confrontational ways to prompt peers
Avoid public shaming

cautions: Attitudes and intentions are self-reported, not observed behaviour.
Social-desirability bias is likely; treat 'good' answers cautiously.
q9 does not ask why some would stay silent, so reasons cannot be assumed.

sectionAnalysis.label: Do campus rules and messages reach students?
sectionAnalysis.purpose: Assess reported awareness of rules, the communication funnel (exposure, recall, actionability), practical guidance and sorting confidence.

patterns.meaning: Many respondents report being unaware of the campus fines before the survey.
actions: Check that the rules are accurate, clearly worded and easy to find
Pair rule communication with convenient disposal

patterns.when: q11 option a or b is common
patterns.meaning: Messages are reported as not noticed, or noticed without recall — a reach or recall gap.
actions: Choose one concrete call-to-action and place it near disposal decisions
Measure recall after a campaign, not the number of posters

patterns.when: q12 option a or b is common and q13 option a or b is common
patterns.meaning: Reported practical guidance and sorting confidence are both low.
actions: Run a short practical demonstration
Use consistent, item-specific labels once the campus streams are verified

cautions: Recall and comprehension are respondent-reported, not an audit of communication frequency or placement.
Confidence is not knowledge, and the survey contains no verified sorting answer key.
Do not infer the college is doing enough or too little from a single question.

sectionAnalysis.label: What could help, and what to test next
sectionAnalysis.purpose: Identify perceived barriers, preferred practical improvements, channels and messages, and concrete participation intentions.

patterns.when: q15 option a or q16 option a is prominent
patterns.meaning: Respondents repeatedly prioritise bins, placement and labels.
actions: Audit bins and collection schedules
Prioritise the leading perceived hotspot
Pair infrastructure with clear instructions

patterns.when: q15 option b or q16 option b is prominent, with q12/q13 uncertainty
patterns.meaning: Responses point toward practical education and guidance.
actions: Run a short practical demonstration
Use clear item-specific visuals and check understanding

patterns.when: q15 option c or q16 option c is prominent
patterns.meaning: Responses point toward norms and visible peer-led habits.
actions: Run a small voluntary peer-led activity
Make correct disposal visible without shaming

patterns.meaning: A notable share prefer stricter enforcement; this states a preference, not that enforcement works.
actions: Verify the actual rules, penalties and how they are applied before acting
Avoid leaning on enforcement alone if bins are inaccessible

patterns.when: q17 and q18 each have a clear leading option
patterns.meaning: A preferred channel and message can be piloted as a hypothesis, not a proven combination.
actions: Pilot the combination
Track reach, recall and outcomes separately

patterns.when: q16 option c or q19 option c/d is prominent
patterns.meaning: There may be an opening for a voluntary student-led pilot.
actions: Invite volunteers with a specific, low-effort ask
Track sign-ups and actual attendance

cautions: Preferred intervention is not necessarily the most effective or affordable.
Stated willingness is not actual participation.
Preferences are hypotheses, not evidence of effectiveness.

dimensions.meaning: How often respondents report seeing problems and which broad areas they name.
Whether access, capacity, labels or placement recur across answers.
Whether disapproval, perceived peer norms and willingness to intervene point the same way.
Whether rules and messages are noticed/remembered and whether guidance and confidence feel adequate.
Which improvements, channels, messages and participation forms respondents favour.

synthesisRules.when: an infrastructure barrier and the practical guidance gap both appear
synthesisRules.summary: A combined approach may be warranted: make correct disposal convenient and provide clear instructions at the point of disposal.

synthesisRules.when: the funnel recall gap or the awareness gap appears
synthesisRules.summary: Test message visibility, recall and clarity before simply producing more posters.
Try a small voluntary student-led pilot; confirm interest through actual sign-ups and attendance.

synthesisRules.when: no rule has enough support or leading options are closely split
synthesisRules.summary: Do not force a single conclusion. Report the split and consider a low-cost combined pilot or further targeted observation.

reportSections: Do campus rules and messages reach students?
What could help, and what to test next

students.action: Use an appropriate bin where available; when practical, keep waste until a suitable disposal point is found.
students.caveat: Do not place all responsibility on students if bins are inaccessible, full or unclear.

students.action: Use polite, non-confrontational reminders or join voluntary activities.

college.action: Audit placement, capacity, overflow, labels and collection schedules in perceived hotspots.
college.caveat: Validate perceptions with observation before costly changes.

college.action: Provide consistent, item-specific labels and demonstrations that match actual campus waste handling.
college.caveat: Confirm local collection rules before publishing sorting guidance.

college.action: Make current waste rules accurate, clear and easy to find; verify any penalty wording before communicating it.

thegreenfeed.action: Pilot one clear message through the leading preferred channel and measure recall.
thegreenfeed.caveat: Preference and recall do not prove behaviour change.

thegreenfeed.action: Run a small voluntary activity and track sign-ups, attendance and feedback.
thegreenfeed.caveat: Do not infer attendance from stated willingness.

thegreenfeed.action: Repeat a short measurement after a pilot and add direct observation where possible.
thegreenfeed.caveat: Without a suitable comparison design, changes cannot be attributed solely to the campaign.

metrics: Option counts and percentages per question

limitations: This is deterministic descriptive analysis, not a validated psychometric instrument or causal model.
The questionnaire only supports interpretations its wording/options reasonably allow; do not invent unasked reasons.
Recall, social desirability, selection bias and uneven participation can affect results.
Respondents are not automatically representative of all PCTE students.
Report what a pattern is consistent with, not what it proves.
Claims of improvement require follow-up measurements and preferably direct observation.
Programme-level comparisons can mislead when group sizes differ or are very small.
Sorting confidence is not sorting knowledge; the survey contains no verified answer key.
The v4 instrument collects different questions from v3; the two versions must never be merged into one distribution.
